title: Do teachers dream of electric students?
author: Tom Bennett
summary: Tom Bennett publishes his original Telegraph piece on the AV1, a camera-equipped robot avatar that sits in English classrooms on behalf of children who cannot or will not attend school. He grants that the device may be useful for children kept home by cancer treatment or other serious illness, but turns his attention to its more controversial use for emotionally based school avoidance. His key argument is that schools and councils have built vocabulary and infrastructure around a condition with no agreed diagnostic threshold, and that genuine distress is not the same as a mental health disorder. Bennett contends that the standard route back to school is a stepped reintegration with gentle pressure, and that a robot used as a long-term substitute for attendance risks reinforcing avoidance rather than dismantling it. He also raises privacy, safeguarding and classroom management concerns, and questions the manufacturer's claim that 76% of users return to school in the absence of any comparison group. He concludes that pilots with high entitlement thresholds are sensible, but that children need to be physically in school whenever possible.
points: Bennett notes that 1.34 million children in England (18%) were persistently absent in 2024/25, well above pre-pandemic levels.
He warns that there is no nationally agreed measure or diagnostic threshold for emotionally based school avoidance, even as provision expands.
Used as a long-term substitute for attendance, the AV1 could reinforce avoidance instead of supporting stepped reintegration.
The vendor's claim that 76% of AV1 users return to school is challenged for lacking any comparison group.
Broadcasting lessons into and from a child's bedroom raises serious privacy and safeguarding issues.
quotes: The AV1 robot is a different kind of digital native that sits in a real classroom, fitted with cameras and microphones, allowing their human operatives to watch and participate in lessons.
The sticky bit is that we’ve created a vocabulary and infrastructure around something we don’t even measure very well.
You can experience genuine distress without it being a mental health disorder. Some things are hard; life frequently is. Learning is hard work.
If students see it as a substitute for going in, on a long-term basis, then the school avoidance becomes reinforced rather than dismantled.
There are huge privacy and safeguarding issues when you are broadcasting from and into someone’s bedroom.
The company behind it claims that 76% of students using the AV1 return to school. But compared to what?
Without good data, we’re shooting in the dark, using other people’s money as bullets and other people’s kids as target practice.
